# Technical Brief: Distributed Consensus and Coordination

## 1. Raft

**Leader election.** Raft divides time into monotonically increasing **terms**, each beginning with an election. A follower that hears no heartbeat within a **randomized election timeout** (typically 150–300 ms, randomized to avoid split votes) transitions to **candidate**, increments its term, votes for itself, and issues **RequestVote RPCs**. A candidate wins with votes from a majority quorum; each server grants at most one vote per term (persisted as `votedFor`), guaranteeing at most one leader per term (**Election Safety**).

**Log replication.** The leader appends client commands to its log and replicates via **AppendEntries RPCs**, which double as heartbeats. Each RPC carries `prevLogIndex`/`prevLogTerm`; a follower rejects the entry unless its log matches at that point, enforcing the **Log Matching Property** (if two logs share an entry with the same index and term, all preceding entries are identical). The leader maintains per-follower `nextIndex`/`matchIndex`, decrementing `nextIndex` on rejection to force divergent follower suffixes to be overwritten. An entry is **committed** when stored on a majority; the leader advances `commitIndex` and followers learn it piggybacked on subsequent AppendEntries.

**Safety mechanisms.** The **Election Restriction** (the "up-to-date" check in RequestVote: compare last log term, then last log index) ensures a candidate cannot win unless its log contains all committed entries, yielding the **Leader Completeness Property**. Crucially, a leader never commits entries from prior terms by counting replicas directly (Figure 8 of Ongaro & Ousterhout's paper shows the counterexample); it commits them only indirectly by committing an entry from its *current* term. Together these give the **State Machine Safety Property**: no two servers apply different commands at the same log index.

## 2. Paxos

**Single-Decree (Basic) Paxos.** Lamport's protocol decides one value using two phases over **proposers**, **acceptors**, and **learners**. In **Phase 1 (Prepare/Promise)**, a proposer sends `Prepare(n)` with a unique, totally ordered proposal number; an acceptor promises never to accept proposals numbered below *n* and returns the highest-numbered proposal it has accepted. In **Phase 2 (Accept/Accepted)**, the proposer sends `Accept(n, v)`, where *v* must be the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal reported in Phase 1 (or any value if none)—this **value-picking rule** plus **majority quorum intersection** (any two majorities share an acceptor) is what preserves safety across competing proposers. Liveness is not guaranteed: dueling proposers can livelock, which is exactly the escape hatch FLP (§8) requires.

**Multi-Paxos.** Running Basic Paxos per log slot is wasteful, so Multi-Paxos elects a **distinguished proposer (stable leader)** that executes Phase 1 once over an unbounded range of instances; thereafter each command needs only one Phase 2 round trip (one round trip to a quorum), matching Raft's steady-state cost. Leadership is typically maintained with a lease (§3) to avoid competing proposers.

**Variants.** **Fast Paxos** lets clients send proposals directly to acceptors in "fast rounds," saving a message delay but requiring larger **fast quorums** (e.g., ⌈3n/4⌉) and a collision-recovery mechanism. **Cheap Paxos** uses f auxiliary acceptors that participate only during failures, so steady state needs only f+1 main acceptors. **Flexible Paxos (FPaxos)** (Howard, Malkhi, Spiegelman) generalizes the quorum requirement: only Phase-1 quorums (Q1) and Phase-2 quorums (Q2) must intersect (|Q1| + |Q2| > n), not Q2 with Q2—enabling, e.g., small write quorums with large election quorums. **EPaxos (Egalitarian Paxos)** is leaderless: any replica commits commands in one round trip when commands don't conflict, tracking a **dependency graph** and ordering conflicting commands at execution time.

## 3. Lease-Based Coordination

**Gray & Cheriton leases.** The foundational mechanism (1989, originally for distributed file-cache consistency): a **lease** is a time-bounded grant of authority. Safety rests on an assumption of **bounded clock drift (ρ)** between grantor and holder; the holder conservatively expires its lease earlier than the grantor does. Unlike locks, leases are fault-tolerant by construction—if the holder crashes, the resource becomes available after expiry without any recovery protocol.

**Chubby locks and sequencers.** Google's **Chubby** service exposes **coarse-grained advisory locks** backed by a Multi-Paxos replicated cell. Because a lock holder can pause (GC, scheduling) and act after its lease has expired, Chubby issues a **sequencer**—an opaque token naming the lock, mode, and **lock generation number**—that downstream servers validate before honoring requests. This is the canonical defense against the **stale lease-holder** problem.

**Fencing tokens.** The generalization (articulated by Kleppmann in the Redlock debate): every lease grant carries a **monotonically increasing fencing token**, and every protected resource rejects requests bearing a token lower than the highest it has seen. This converts a lease from a timing-dependent mutual-exclusion claim into a safe ordering mechanism even under arbitrary process pauses. Lock services whose tokens are not monotonic (e.g., Redis **Redlock** across independent masters) cannot provide this guarantee under clock skew or pauses.

**Leader leases for local reads.** Raft and Multi-Paxos deployments (etcd, Spanner) use **leader leases** so the leader can serve **linearizable reads locally** without a quorum round trip (avoiding the cost of Raft's alternative, the **ReadIndex** protocol). Spanner binds leader leases to **TrueTime** intervals, with disjointness enforced by the invariant that a new lease cannot begin until the old one's maximum timestamp has provably passed. The tradeoff throughout: leases trade **liveness** (must wait out expiry after a crash) for **safety** achieved with only bounded-clock-rate assumptions.

## 4. Membership Changes (Reconfiguration)

**Raft joint consensus.** To move from configuration C_old to C_new, the leader first commits a transitional configuration **C_old,new** in which every decision (elections and commitment) requires **overlapping majorities of both configurations**. Only after C_old,new commits does the leader commit C_new. This prevents the classic hazard of two disjoint majorities (one under each configuration) electing independent leaders during the transition. Configuration entries take effect when *appended*, not committed.

**Raft single-server changes.** The simpler scheme adds/removes one server at a time, exploiting the fact that any majority of C_old and any majority of C_new intersect when they differ by one member. Ongaro later documented a **safety bug** in the originally published version (two concurrent single-server changes starting from different base configurations can produce disjoint quorums) and the fix: a leader may begin a configuration change only after committing an entry (e.g., a no-op) **in its current term**. Related mechanisms: **catch-up phase** (new servers join as non-voting learners until their logs catch up) and **leader step-down** when the leader removes itself.

**Paxos α-reconfiguration and Vertical Paxos.** In Lamport's "Paxos Made Simple"/SMR tradition, the configuration is itself state-machine state: the configuration used for log slot *i* is determined by the configuration command committed at slot *i − α*, bounding pipeline concurrency by α. **Vertical Paxos** (Lamport, Malkhi, Zhou) instead delegates reconfiguration to an external **auxiliary master** (itself a small consensus service), allowing each "ballot" to use a different configuration—this is the theoretical underpinning of primary-backup systems reconfigured by a Chubby/ZooKeeper-like coordinator.

**SWIM gossip membership.** For weakly consistent membership (as in Serf/Consul's LAN pool and Cassandra-style systems), **SWIM** separates **failure detection** (randomized periodic ping, then **indirect ping** via k proxies) from **dissemination** (piggybacking membership updates on ping traffic, an **infection-style/gossip** broadcast). The **suspicion mechanism** marks nodes *suspect* before *dead*, letting a falsely accused node refute via an **incarnation number**, drastically cutting false positives. **Lifeguard** (HashiCorp) further adapts timeouts to local slowness.

## 5. Consistency Models

**Linearizability** (Herlihy & Wing, 1990). The gold standard for single-object consistency: every operation appears to take effect **atomically at a single point between its invocation and response**, consistent with **real-time order**—if op A completes before op B begins, A precedes B in the linearization. It is **composable (local)**: a system of linearizable objects is linearizable. It is what Raft/Multi-Paxos state machines provide, and what the CAP theorem's "C" formally means. Verification is NP-hard in general (checked in practice by tools like Jepsen/Knossos/Porcupine).

**Sequential consistency** (Lamport, 1979). All processes observe the *same* total order of operations, and each process's operations appear in its program order—but there is **no real-time constraint** across processes. Strictly weaker than linearizability and, notably, **not composable**. ZooKeeper's default guarantee is close to this: writes are linearizable (via Zab), but reads are served locally and may be stale, yielding sequential-consistency-like behavior per session (with `sync()` to upgrade a read).

**Causal consistency and causal+.** Operations related by **potential causality** (Lamport's happens-before: program order, reads-from, transitivity) must be observed in order; concurrent operations may be seen in different orders by different replicas. **COPS** introduced **causal+** (causal consistency plus **convergent conflict handling**) and showed causal consistency is the strongest model achievable in an **always-available, partition-tolerant** ("ALPS") system—the sweet spot below the CAP line. Implementations track causality with **vector clocks** or explicit dependency metadata.

**Eventual/strong eventual consistency and session guarantees.** **Eventual consistency** promises only convergence absent new writes; **strong eventual consistency** (Shapiro et al.) strengthens it via **CRDTs** (state-based CvRDTs with join-semilattice merge; op-based CmRDTs with commutative operations—e.g., G-Counter, PN-Counter, OR-Set), guaranteeing deterministic convergence without consensus. The **session guarantees** of Terry et al. (Bayou)—**read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes-follow-reads**—give per-client sanity atop weak models; together they are equivalent to causal consistency per session.

## 6. Failure Modes

**Crash-stop vs. crash-recovery vs. omission.** The **crash-stop** model (process halts forever) is what classic consensus proofs assume; real systems need the **crash-recovery** model, which forces **durable state** (Raft persists `currentTerm`, `votedFor`, and the log; Paxos acceptors persist promises and accepted values) and makes **fsync semantics and torn writes** a correctness concern. **Omission failures** (dropped messages) are subsumed by the asynchronous network assumption.

**Byzantine faults.** Processes may behave arbitrarily—lying, equivocating, colluding. Tolerating *f* Byzantine faults requires **n ≥ 3f + 1** replicas (see §8) and authenticated, multi-phase protocols: **PBFT** (Castro & Liskov) runs **pre-prepare → prepare → commit** with 2f+1 quorums and **view changes** to replace a faulty primary, at O(n²) message complexity; **HotStuff** linearizes communication and enables chained/pipelined rotation of leaders (basis of LibraBFT/DiemBFT). Crash-tolerant protocols like Raft are *unsafe* under Byzantine behavior.

**Network partitions and split-brain.** Partitions force the CAP tradeoff (§8). **Split-brain**—two sub-clusters each believing they hold authority—is prevented in quorum systems by **majority quorums** (a minority partition cannot elect or commit) and in storage systems by **fencing** (§3, e.g., STONITH in HA clusters). Asymmetric partitions motivate refinements like Raft's **Pre-Vote** (a candidate checks electability before incrementing its term) and **CheckQuorum/leader lease stickiness** to stop a partitioned node from disrupting a healthy leader with inflated terms.

**Gray failures and fail-slow hardware.** Huang et al. define **gray failure** by **differential observability**: the system's internal detectors see the component as healthy while clients experience failure (e.g., a NIC dropping 1% of packets, a disk running at 1% speed—"fail-slow at scale," Gunawi et al.). These evade binary failure detectors and motivate richer health signals and SWIM/Lifeguard-style adaptive detection.

**Clock skew and timing failures.** Unsynchronized clocks break naive lease and timestamp schemes (§3). Spanner's **TrueTime** exposes bounded uncertainty intervals TT.now() = [earliest, latest] (GPS + atomic clocks) and enforces external consistency via **commit wait** (hold a commit until its timestamp's uncertainty has passed). Systems without such bounds must treat wall clocks as advisory (hence hybrid logical clocks, HLC, in CockroachDB).

## 7. Atomic Broadcast (Total-Order Broadcast)

**Equivalence to consensus.** Chandra & Toueg proved **atomic broadcast and consensus are equivalent** in asynchronous systems with crash failures: each is reducible to the other. Atomic broadcast requires **validity, (uniform) agreement, integrity, and total order**—all correct processes deliver the same messages in the same order. This is why "replicated log" and "consensus" are used interchangeably in practice.

**Zab (ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast).** Zab is a **primary-backup atomic broadcast** protocol. Transactions carry **zxids** = ⟨epoch, counter⟩. The protocol runs three phases: **discovery** (elect a prospective leader; collect the highest accepted epoch from a quorum), **synchronization** (the new leader brings a quorum of followers to a consistent prefix before broadcasting), and **broadcast** (two-phase, leader-driven proposal/ACK/COMMIT). Zab's distinguishing guarantee over vanilla Multi-Paxos is **primary order (PO causality)**: all state changes from one primary are delivered in the exact order issued, with no interleaving from a prior epoch—important because ZooKeeper replicates *state deltas*, not idempotent commands.

**Viewstamped Replication (VR).** Oki & Liskov's protocol (1988, predating the Paxos paper's publication) totally orders requests via a **primary** within a **view**; each operation gets an **op-number**, and the primary commits after **PrepareOK** from a quorum. On suspected primary failure, a **view change** elects the node with the most advanced log (selected by ⟨view-number, op-number⟩) as the next primary—structurally the ancestor of Raft's design. **VR Revisited** (Liskov & Cowling, 2012) adds a **recovery protocol** allowing crash-recovery without stable storage for the log.

**Virtual synchrony (Isis).** Birman's model couples group membership with ordered multicast: messages are delivered within **views**, and **view-synchronous delivery** guarantees all surviving members deliver the same message set before installing a new view. Ordering flavors include **FIFO, causal (CBCAST), and total order (ABCAST)**. This lineage powers group-communication systems (Isis, Horus, Spread, JGroups) and modern derivatives (Derecho). The key contrast with Paxos-style SMR: virtual synchrony can use **amnesia-free progress within a primary partition** and historically favored speed over strict durability.

**Modern log-replication instances.** **Kafka's** replication (ISR—in-sync replica set, with **KRaft** now replacing ZooKeeper for metadata consensus) and **Apache BookKeeper** (fencing-based ledger closure) are production atomic-broadcast-shaped systems, each ultimately reducible to the consensus core above.

## 8. Impossibility Results and Lower Bounds

**FLP impossibility** (Fischer, Lynch, Paterson, 1985). No **deterministic** protocol solves consensus in an **asynchronous** system if even **one process may crash**. The proof is topological in flavor: any protocol has an initial **bivalent configuration** (both outcomes still possible), and from any bivalent configuration an adversarial scheduler can always delay the "critical" message to reach another bivalent configuration, constructing an infinite non-deciding execution. FLP does not forbid consensus in practice; it forbids *guaranteed termination*. The three canonical **circumventions**: (a) **randomization** — Ben-Or's protocol terminates with probability 1 by coin-flipping out of bivalence; (b) **partial synchrony** — Dwork, Lynch & Stockmeyer (DLS, 1988) showed consensus is solvable if the system is eventually synchronous after an unknown **Global Stabilization Time (GST)**, which is exactly the model Raft, Multi-Paxos, and PBFT assume (safety always, liveness after GST); (c) **unreliable failure detectors** — Chandra, Hadzilacos & Toueg proved **Ω** (eventual leader election, equivalently ◇W) is the **weakest failure detector** for consensus, and **◇S** suffices with a majority of correct processes.

**CAP theorem.** Brewer's 2000 conjecture, proved by **Gilbert & Lynch (2002)**: in an asynchronous network, no read/write register can guarantee all three of **Consistency (linearizability), Availability (every request to a non-failed node gets a response), and Partition tolerance**. Since partitions are not optional, the real choice during a partition is **C vs. A** (CP: majority-side progress only, as in Raft/Spanner; AP: always respond, reconcile later, as in Dynamo). Abadi's **PACELC** refinement adds the no-partition tradeoff: **Else, Latency vs. Consistency** (e.g., Spanner's commit wait pays latency for consistency even absent partitions). Note the common misreadings: CAP's "C" is linearizability, not ACID consistency, and "A" is a specific formal property, not uptime.

**Two Generals problem** (Akkoyunlu et al. 1975; popularized by Gray 1978). **No protocol achieves guaranteed common knowledge of agreement over an unreliable link**: by induction, the last message of any purported protocol might be lost, so its sender's state cannot depend on it, so it can be elided—collapsing the protocol. This is why **exactly-once delivery** over a lossy network is impossible in the strict sense and why practical systems substitute **at-least-once delivery + idempotence/deduplication**, and why distributed transactions use **2PC with a (blocking) coordinator** rather than symmetric agreement. (Relatedly, **2PC blocks** on coordinator failure; **3PC** fixes blocking only under synchrony and no partitions—another shadow of FLP.)

**Byzantine agreement lower bounds** (Lamport, Shostak, Pease, 1980/82). Without message authentication, Byzantine agreement requires **n ≥ 3f + 1** processes to tolerate *f* traitors (the **3-general impossibility**: with n = 3, f = 1, a loyal general cannot distinguish which peer is lying). With **digital signatures**, agreement is possible for any n ≥ f + 2, but the **connectivity bound** (> 2f) and the **f + 1 round lower bound** for deterministic agreement (Fischer–Lynch) still apply. These bounds dictate PBFT/HotStuff replica counts (4 nodes for f = 1) and quorum sizes (2f + 1 of 3f + 1).

**Atomic-register and ordering bounds (supporting results).** Attiya, Bar-Noy & Dolev's **ABD** algorithm shows linearizable registers *are* achievable with a majority in asynchrony (consensus is strictly harder—**consensus number** hierarchy, Herlihy's wait-free hierarchy: registers have consensus number 1, CAS has ∞), and Lamport's "lower bounds on asynchronous consensus" establishes the **2-message-delay minimum** for learning a decided value, which Fast Paxos meets at the cost of larger quorums.

---

**Synthesis.** The field is organized around one spine: FLP and the Two Generals problem bound what is achievable; partial synchrony, randomization, and failure detectors define the escape hatches; Paxos/Raft/VR/Zab are engineering instantiations of consensus ≡ atomic broadcast in the partial-synchrony model; leases and fencing tokens extend consensus-derived authority through time under bounded-clock assumptions; reconfiguration protocols (joint consensus, α-windows, Vertical Paxos) keep quorum intersection invariant while the quorum set itself changes; and consistency models (linearizability down to eventual/CRDT convergence) name the precise guarantees these machines export to clients, with CAP/PACELC pricing each level against availability and latency under the failure modes—crash, Byzantine, partition, gray, and timing—that real deployments actually exhibit.

Answer: The brief above covers all eight areas with ≥3 named mechanisms each: (1) Raft — randomized-timeout leader election/RequestVote, AppendEntries log replication with the Log Matching Property, and the Election Restriction/Leader Completeness safety rules; (2) Paxos — Basic Paxos Prepare/Promise–Accept/Accepted with quorum intersection, Multi-Paxos stable leader, and Fast/Cheap/Flexible/EPaxos variants; (3) leases — Gray–Cheriton leases, Chubby sequencers, fencing tokens, and leader leases/ReadIndex/TrueTime; (4) membership — Raft joint consensus, single-server changes (with Ongaro's fix), Paxos α/Vertical Paxos, and SWIM suspicion; (5) consistency — linearizability, sequential, causal/causal+ (COPS), and eventual/CRDTs with session guarantees; (6) failures — crash-recovery, Byzantine (PBFT/HotStuff), partitions/split-brain (Pre-Vote, CheckQuorum), gray/fail-slow, and clock skew (TrueTime); (7) atomic broadcast — Zab, Viewstamped Replication, virtual synchrony, and the Chandra–Toueg consensus equivalence; (8) impossibility — FLP (with Ben-Or/DLS/Ω circumventions), CAP/PACELC, Two Generals, and the 3f+1 and f+1-round Byzantine lower bounds.
